name: Git

modules.title: Git Foundations
modules.description: Understand what Git records, why it is distributed, and how snapshots, objects, and references fit together.
modules.challenge: Create a disposable repository, make two snapshots, and explain where the working tree, index, and history differ.

history.title: Git in 60 seconds
history.summary: Git was created for fast, distributed Linux kernel development and grew into the version-control foundation used by projects of every size.

milestones.title: Patches & archives
milestones.description: Early Linux kernel changes were shared as patches and archived files.

milestones.title: BitKeeper era
milestones.description: The Linux kernel project adopted the distributed BitKeeper system for its development history.

milestones.title: Git is created
milestones.description: Linus Torvalds created Git after BitKeeper access changed; the open-source system has continued to mature.

history.flow: edit files -> stage a snapshot -> commit locally -> share with a remote

modules.title: Install, Configure & Get Help
modules.description: Set up Git deliberately so new repositories, commits, editors, and credentials behave predictably.
modules.challenge: Install Git, set repository-safe identity and defaults, then locate help for an unfamiliar command.

modules.title: Repositories & File States
modules.description: Create or copy repositories and read the tracked, untracked, modified, staged, and ignored states correctly.
modules.challenge: Initialize a sample project, classify every file state with status, and safely rename and remove tracked files.

modules.title: Staging & Commits
modules.description: Shape small, reviewable snapshots with intentional staging and useful commit messages.
modules.challenge: Split mixed edits into two atomic commits and verify the exact staged diff before each commit.

modules.title: Inspect History & Changes
modules.description: Read commit history and compare snapshots without changing repository state.
modules.challenge: Trace when a behavior changed, inspect its patch, and summarize the files affected across a commit range.

modules.title: Branches, HEAD & Switching
modules.description: Use lightweight branches confidently and understand exactly what switching changes.
modules.challenge: Create a feature branch, make it track a remote branch, inspect divergence, and remove it safely after integration.

modules.title: Merging
modules.description: Integrate branch histories and recognize fast-forward, three-way, and explicit merge commits.
modules.challenge: Merge two sample branches using fast-forward and non-fast-forward cases, then inspect the resulting graph.

modules.title: Remotes & Collaboration
modules.description: Exchange commits and references with other repositories while keeping fetch, merge, and push responsibilities clear.
modules.challenge: Add a remote, fetch it, compare remote-tracking history, publish a branch, and prune obsolete references.

modules.title: Rebase & Cherry-pick
modules.description: Replay commits intentionally to update or refine a branch without confusing shared collaborators.
modules.challenge: Rebase a private feature branch onto updated main, squash fixups interactively, and move one isolated fix with cherry-pick.

modules.title: Undoing & Recovery
modules.description: Choose restore, reset, revert, reflog, or clean according to whether work is staged, committed, shared, or untracked.
modules.challenge: Recover a discarded branch in a disposable repository and demonstrate a safe public revert without rewriting shared history.

modules.title: Tags, Releases & Archives
modules.description: Name release points, verify them, describe nearby builds, and export source snapshots.
modules.challenge: Create an annotated release tag, push only that tag, generate a version string, and export a source archive.

modules.title: Ignore Rules, Attributes & Line Endings
modules.description: Keep generated files out of commits and make path-specific content behavior consistent across platforms.
modules.challenge: Design project and personal ignore rules, diagnose one ignored path, and normalize text line endings with attributes.

modules.title: Stash & Multiple Worktrees
modules.description: Temporarily set work aside or check out another branch without mixing unrelated changes.
modules.challenge: Pause an unfinished change, fix an urgent issue in a second worktree, then restore the original work safely.

modules.title: Search, Blame & Bisect
modules.description: Use repository history as a debugging tool instead of manually scanning files and commits.
modules.challenge: Locate when a constant changed, identify the responsible line history, and bisect a reproducible regression.

modules.title: Conflict Resolution
modules.description: Resolve content and structural conflicts deliberately during merge, rebase, cherry-pick, and stash operations.
modules.challenge: Create a controlled conflict, inspect all three index stages, resolve it, verify the result, and finish the operation.

modules.title: Submodules, Large Repositories & Portability
modules.description: Compose repositories carefully and reduce checkout cost when projects or binary assets become large.
modules.challenge: Add a pinned library submodule, clone it recursively, and compare submodules with sparse checkout and Git LFS trade-offs.

modules.title: Hooks, Signing & Security
modules.description: Automate local checks, verify history, protect credentials, and understand where Git trust ends.
modules.challenge: Create a fast pre-commit check, sign one commit in a disposable repository, and document secret-handling rules for the team.

modules.title: Team Workflows & CI/CD
modules.description: Turn Git mechanics into a reviewable team workflow with protected integration and reproducible delivery.
modules.challenge: Design a small-team workflow from issue and branch through review, tested merge, immutable release tag, and rollback.

1: Version control records meaningful file changes over time so a team can compare, restore, and collaborate safely.
Every normal Git clone contains repository history, so most inspection and commit work happens locally.
The repository stores Git history and metadata; the working tree is the checked-out set of files you edit.
A commit records a snapshot of tracked content plus metadata and parent links rather than merely saving a list of edit commands.
Blobs store file content, trees describe directories, commits point to trees and parents, and annotated tags name objects with metadata.
Branches and tags are readable references to objects, while HEAD identifies the currently checked-out branch or commit.
Edits begin in the working tree, selected content enters the index, and commit stores that staged snapshot in the repository.
working tree -> git add -> index -> git commit -> repository
2: Check the installed Git version before relying on newer commands or options.
System, global, local, worktree, and command scopes layer configuration from broad defaults to narrow overrides.
user.name and user.email become commit metadata; they are not authentication credentials for a hosting provider.

git config --global user.name "Ada Developer"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
init.defaultBranch controls the initial branch name used by newly initialized repositories.
Git can use configured editor and pager programs for commit messages and long command output.
Aliases shorten repeated commands but should remain understandable to teammates and your future self.
Git exposes manual pages and concise option summaries directly from the command line.
3: git init creates the .git directory that turns an existing folder into a repository.
git clone copies repository data, creates a working tree, and normally configures origin and a remote-tracking branch.
Tracked files belong to a committed or staged snapshot; untracked files have not yet entered Git history.
A tracked file can have one version in HEAD, another in the index, and another in the working tree.
Ignore rules keep generated or local-only untracked paths out of ordinary status and add operations.
git mv stages a delete at the old path and an add at the new path; Git later detects the rename from content similarity.
git rm removes a path from the working tree and stages its removal; --cached keeps the local file.
4: git add stages the current content of selected paths; later edits remain unstaged until added again.
Patch mode lets you choose individual change hunks so unrelated edits do not enter the same commit.
git diff --staged shows the exact patch the next commit would record.
A commit stores the staged tree, author and committer metadata, message, and parent relationship.
A useful subject states the change as a concise action; a body can explain motivation, constraints, and consequences.

git commit
# Add retry limit
#
# Prevent repeated provider calls after terminal failures.
Amend replaces the latest commit with a new one containing the current index and optionally a new message.
An atomic commit contains one coherent change that can be reviewed, reverted, or moved independently.

git add -p
git commit -m "Fix timeout handling"
5: git log walks reachable commits and can limit results by author, date, message, path, or revision range.
A graph view makes branch, merge, and tag relationships visible alongside abbreviated commits.
git show displays an object; for a commit it includes metadata and the introduced patch.
git diff compares unstaged working-tree content with the index by default.
Two revisions can be compared directly; A..B selects commits reachable from B but not A for log-style traversal.

git diff main...feature/login
git log main..feature/login
Statistics and name-status views reveal scope before you inspect a full patch.

git diff --stat main...HEAD
git diff --name-status main...HEAD
Adding -- before a path separates revisions from paths and narrows history to that file or directory.
6: A local branch is a movable reference to a commit, not a separate copy of project files.
HEAD normally points symbolically to the current branch, whose reference advances when you commit.
git switch -c creates a branch at the chosen start point and checks it out in one step.
Checking out a commit directly detaches HEAD; new commits remain recoverable but are not kept by a branch unless you create one.
Rename updates a local branch name; safe deletion refuses while commits remain unmerged.

git branch -m old-name better-name
git branch -d merged-branch
An upstream connects a local branch to the remote-tracking branch used by status, pull, and argument-free push behavior.
The merge base is a best common ancestor used to reason about where two lines of development diverged.
7: If the current branch is an ancestor of the other branch, Git can advance its reference without creating a merge commit.
Diverged branches require Git to combine both tips using their common ancestor as the baseline.
A merge commit has multiple parents and records that histories were integrated at that point.
--no-ff preserves an explicit integration commit even when a fast-forward would be possible.
Strategy options such as renormalization or favoring one side affect how specific conflicts are resolved; they do not replace review.
Fetch and compare the candidate branch before merging so scope and test expectations are understood.

git fetch origin
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main
git diff --stat HEAD...origin/main
When a merge cannot be completed safely, --abort attempts to restore the pre-merge state.
8: A remote is a named set of URLs and refspecs for another repository; origin is only a conventional name.
Remote commands manage fetch and push URLs without altering existing commit objects.
git fetch downloads objects and updates configured remote-tracking references without integrating them into your current branch.
A name such as origin/main records the last fetched position of main in the origin repository.
git pull fetches and then integrates according to configuration, usually with merge or rebase; fetch-first is easier to inspect.
Push sends objects and updates allowed remote references; -u records the upstream for later status and push commands.
Pruning removes remote-tracking references whose source branches were deleted from the remote.
9: Rebase finds commits unique to a branch and reapplies their changes onto a new base, producing new commit IDs.
--onto precisely selects a new base, an old base boundary, and the branch whose commits should move.
Interactive rebase can reorder, edit, combine, relabel, or remove commits before they are shared.
squash combines messages, fixup discards the later message, and reword changes a message while preserving its patch.

git commit --fixup HEAD~2
git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~5
After resolving a rebase stop, continue records the resolution; skip omits that patch; abort restores the original branch.
Cherry-pick applies the change introduced by selected commits onto the current branch as new commits.
Avoid rebasing commits others already depend on unless the team coordinates the rewrite and uses force-with-lease safely.
10: git restore replaces selected working-tree content from the index or another source; uncommitted edits can be lost.
--staged copies the selected path from HEAD into the index while leaving the working-tree edit intact.
--soft moves the branch only, default mixed reset also resets the index, and --hard also replaces working-tree content.
git revert creates a new commit that applies the inverse of an earlier commit, preserving published history.
Reflogs record recent local reference movements and often reveal commits no longer named by a branch.
Once a commit ID is found in the reflog, create a branch immediately to keep it reachable.
git clean permanently removes untracked paths; preview with -n and include ignored files only with deliberate scope.

git clean -nd
# review before: git clean -fd
11: A lightweight tag is a fixed reference directly to an object, useful as a simple private marker.
An annotated tag is its own object with tagger, date, message, and optional signature; releases usually benefit from this metadata.
Tag patterns and sorting make version families easier to inspect in a repository with many releases.
git show reveals annotated-tag metadata and the referenced commit or object.
Tags are not automatically pushed with normal branch updates; publish a named tag or intentionally use --follow-tags.
git describe derives a readable identifier from the nearest reachable annotated tag plus later commit distance.
git archive exports tracked content from a tree without repository metadata or ignored working files.
12: A repository .gitignore shares rules for intentionally untracked files such as build output, caches, and local configuration.
A leading ! re-includes a path when its parent directory remains visible; a trailing slash targets directories.
Command-line rules, per-directory .gitignore files, repository excludes, and global excludes apply with defined precedence.
Ignore rules affect untracked paths; remove an already tracked secret or generated file from the index separately.
check-ignore reports the exact pattern and source file responsible for ignoring a path.
Attributes assign text, diff, merge, export, and filter behavior to path patterns under version control.
A text attribute with an explicit eol keeps repository content normalized while checking out suitable platform line endings.
13: stash push saves tracked working-tree and index changes as stash commits and resets them from the worktree.
Stashes are reflog entries; inspect their summary or patch before choosing one to restore.

git stash list
git stash show -p stash@{0}
apply restores a stash without deleting it; pop removes it only after a successful application.
-u also stashes untracked files, while ignored files remain unless the stronger --all option is used.
git stash push -u -m "WIP with new files"
stash branch creates a branch at the stash's original base and applies the work where it is least likely to conflict.
A linked worktree checks out another branch in a separate directory while sharing the same repository object database.
List linked worktrees before removing one; removal refuses when uncommitted work would be lost unless forced.

git worktree list
git worktree remove ../app-hotfix
14: git grep searches tracked content quickly and can limit matches by revision, path, context, or pattern type.
git log -S finds commits where the number of occurrences of an exact string changed.
git log -G finds commits whose patch contains added or removed lines matching a regular expression.
git blame shows the last commit that changed each selected line, providing a starting point rather than assigning personal fault.
git bisect repeatedly checks a midpoint between known good and bad revisions to isolate the first bad commit.

git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good v1.1.0
bisect run executes a deterministic command at each candidate commit and classifies zero as good and nonzero as bad.
range-diff compares two versions of a commit series, useful after rebasing or revising a review branch.
15: A conflict occurs when Git cannot safely combine changes, such as overlapping edits or competing delete and modify operations.
Text conflicts mark the current side, separator, and incoming side; edit the file into the single intended result.

<<<<<<< HEAD
current change
=======
incoming change
>>>>>>> feature
During a merge conflict the index can hold the common base, ours, and theirs as stages 1, 2, and 3.
The meaning of ours and theirs depends on the operation, especially during rebase, so confirm before choosing a side wholesale.

git checkout --ours -- path/to/file
git checkout --theirs -- path/to/file
After editing and testing the final content, git add replaces unmerged index stages with the resolved version.
Merge is completed with commit, while rebase and cherry-pick use their respective --continue commands.
rerere can remember how a conflict was resolved and propose the same resolution when an identical conflict returns.
16: A submodule entry records a specific commit from another repository, while .gitmodules records its path and URL.
submodule add clones the child repository and stages both its gitlink entry and .gitmodules configuration.
--recurse-submodules initializes and checks out nested repositories at the commits recorded by the parent.
Existing clones use update --init --recursive to populate missing submodules at the commits selected by the parent repository.
Updating a submodule means checking out a newer child commit and committing the changed gitlink in the parent.

git -C libs/shared fetch
git -C libs/shared switch --detach v2.0.0
git add libs/shared
Sparse checkout materializes only selected paths in the working tree while the repository can still contain broader history.
Git LFS stores small pointer files in Git while large content is transferred through separate LFS storage supported by the remote.
17: Hooks such as pre-commit and commit-msg run locally at lifecycle points but are not copied automatically by clone.
Receiving repositories can use pre-receive, update, and post-receive hooks to enforce or react to pushed reference changes.
Teams should version hook source in the repository and install it explicitly rather than assuming .git/hooks is shared.
A signed commit attaches a cryptographic signature that others can verify when they trust the corresponding identity.
Signing an annotated release tag protects tag metadata and the object it references from unnoticed substitution.
Verification checks signature validity and reports the signing key; trust policy still belongs to the project.

git verify-commit HEAD
git verify-tag v1.2.0
Never commit passwords, tokens, or private keys; rotation is required even if leaked history is later rewritten.
18: Short-lived branches isolate one change for review and are deleted after their commits reach the integration branch.
Trunk-based teams integrate small changes frequently and use tests or feature flags to keep the main branch releasable.

git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
Hosting-platform reviews discuss a proposed branch integration; Git itself provides the commits and comparison underneath.
A clean series orders prerequisite changes first and keeps mechanical refactoring separate from behavior changes.
Remote branch rules can require review, passing checks, and non-force updates before accepting changes to critical branches.
CI should build and report against an exact commit SHA so results can be tied to immutable source history.
Create releases from reviewed commits and prefer a new revert commit or a prior immutable artifact when rolling back shared production history.

git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release 1.2.0"
git push origin v1.2.0
